conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported by strong randomized-trial evidence, highlighting a 65% relative reduction in invasive breast cancer incidence among postmenopausal women taking exemestane, despite noting short-term limits and non-FDA approval.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

**The claim is supported by strong randomized-trial evidence**, with important limits. In the placebo-controlled MAP.3 trial, 4,560 postmenopausal women at increased breast-cancer risk received exemestane or placebo. At a median follow-up of about 3 years, invasive breast cancer occurred in **11 exemestane recipients versus 32 placebo recipients**: annual incidence **0.19% versus 0.55%**, respectively (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.18–0.70; *P*=0.002). This is a **65% relative reduction** in invasive cancer incidence.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507

That result has good internal validity because it came from a large randomized, placebo-controlled trial. The absolute difference, however, was modest over the observed period—roughly **0.36 fewer invasive cancers per 100 women per year**—and follow-up was relatively short (median 35 months). Thus, the study demonstrates reduced *short-term incidence*, not a proven reduction in breast-cancer mortality or overall mortality.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/

Safety requires individualized assessment. Overall adverse events were more frequent with exemestane (88% vs 85%), though the trial found no statistically significant between-group differences in fractures, cardiovascular events, other cancers, or treatment-related deaths during follow-up.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/Nejmoa1103507

Finally, this is a risk-reduction option rather than an FDA-approved prevention indication: the American Cancer Society notes aromatase inhibitors are not FDA-approved specifically to lower breast-cancer risk, although expert groups include them as options for increased-risk postmenopausal women.  
https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/breast-cancer/risk-and-prevention/aromatase-inhibitors-for-lowering-breast-cancer-risk.html
